children: By Brian Gormley
The venture arm of diabetes research nonprofit Breakthrough T1D was ramping up its efforts to raise $150 million to propel new treatments to market when its leadership collapsed from within.

The T1D Fund, a venture philanthropy, had backed dozens of startups and drawn venture capitalists to Type 1 diabetes. But its efforts also stoked tensions with the Breakthrough brass, which came to believe that some leaders of the T1D Fund were whittling away at Breakthrough's oversight and intent on separating the fund from the foundation.

Breakthrough moved against the T1D Fund in May, firing three of its board members and a member of its investment committee and sharpening its governance of the fund, according to emails and donor communications reviewed by WSJ Pro and people familiar with the events.

In a June letter explaining its actions to board members who were dismissed, reviewed by WSJ Pro, Breakthrough said a subset of the T1D Fund board put the organization at risk by seeking to separate the fund.

Eric Brenner, a lawyer representing fund board members who were fired or resigned, said Breakthrough and the T1D Fund were always separate, with their own boards and officers to ensure independent financial oversight.

The episode shows how differences over management and direction can create tensions between a nonprofit and its venture subsidiary that are hard to overcome. Several nonprofits have launched venture groups to help biotechs advance early-stage science, connect with patients and attract additional investors.

Aaron Kowalski, chief executive of Breakthrough and a member of the T1D Fund board, said Breakthrough's board "acted to protect the interests of donors, the T1D Fund, and ultimately, the mission we all share."
Some former fund board members said Breakthrough's actions shattered the independence that allowed the T1D Fund to thrive.
"It's like they killed the golden goose," said David Nelms, who resigned from the T1D Fund board in protest in May.
More than $100 million in returns

Launched in 2016, the T1D Fund has generated over $100 million in returns by backing biotechs such as Provention Bio, which went public in 2018 and was acquired by drugmaker Sanofi in 2023 for $2.9 billion. Breakthrough's fund raises capital from donors and reinvests returns.

Last year, the fund said it hired Elizabeth Mily, a Bristol-Myers Squibb veteran who could help it make stronger connections with the pharmaceutical industry. The fund then set out to raise $150 million over two years, just as tensions with Breakthrough were coming to a head.

After the T1D Fund board firings, Nelms and two other board members resigned in protest, according to a letter to donors reviewed by WSJ Pro. David Panzirer, a trustee of the Helmsley Charitable Trust, resigned in protest as a board observer.

In its June letter, Breakthrough said, among other things, that some former members had retained counsel to consider the creation of a new nonprofit entity separate from the foundation and refused to grant Breakthrough officers signatory rights on fund investment accounts.

Brenner, the lawyer for T1D Fund board members who were dismissed or resigned, said the fund never blocked any rights. Breakthrough amended the fund's longstanding LLC agreement and gave itself unilateral signatory rights, he added.

The T1D Fund under its reconstituted board said in response that the LLC amendment "simply memorialized existing practice dating back to the fund's inception rather than creating new signing authority." A fund officer, independent of Breakthrough, had full signature authority on fund accounts before and after the amendment, it said.
Members of the T1D Fund board who resigned or were dismissed deny that they tried to separate from the foundation, they said in their own letter sent to donors and reviewed by WSJ Pro.

The fund never hired counsel to explore a separation, according to Jay Eastman, who was the fund's chair until he was fired in May. Instead, for several years it had considered a stand-alone, for-profit vehicle that could raise up to $1 billion to complement the T1D Fund and fuel its portfolio companies with expansion capital, according to Eastman.
It will take far more than what the T1D Fund can raise to propel potential cures to market, Eastman and other members who were dismissed or resigned said.
"This is not a millions problem; it's a billions problem," Eastman said.
'No longer independent'

Some donors pulled or redirected pledges following the board shake-up. The Bukhman Foundation said it withdrew its $12 million donation and the Helmsley Charitable Trust clawed its $3 million gift back, Panzirer said.
"I made it crystal clear: The second the fund is no longer independent, Helmsley is out," Panzirer said.
Anastasia Bukhman, co-founder of the Bukhman Foundation, was one of the fund board members who resigned in protest.
Mily left the fund in June, according to her LinkedIn page. She said she isn't at liberty to comment.

In an August letter to donors reviewed by WSJ Pro, the T1D Fund said that changes to the LLC agreement clarified Breakthrough's role as the fund's sole member, while solidifying the authority of the fund's board to oversee operations and appoint the investment committee, which makes decisions independently.

The T1D Fund said in the letter that capital committed to its $150 million campaign fell to $68 million from $93 million. It now says the vast majority of donors remain with the fund and its fundraising remains on track with more than $75 million raised.
